title: 1 Esdras
subtitle: the Greek Ezra: Josiah's Passover, the return from exile, and the contest of Darius's three guards
lead: 1 Esdras is a Greek book that tells again the last two chapters of 2 Chronicles, nearly all of Ezra and part of Nehemiah 8. It runs from King Josiah's great Passover in Jerusalem (about 622 BC), through the fall of the city to Babylon, the return of the exiles and the rebuilding of the temple, to Ezra's work in Jerusalem and his public reading of the law. Most of it follows the Hebrew books closely, but in a different order, and in the middle it adds a story found nowhere in the Hebrew Bible. Three young bodyguards of the Persian king Darius hold a contest over what is strongest. One says wine, one says the king, and the third, Zerubbabel, says women, and then truth above all. The people shout, "Great is truth, and it is strongest!" (4:41), and Darius rewards the winner with leave to rebuild Jerusalem and its temple (3:1–5:6). The book stops in the middle of a sentence (9:55). It has 9 chapters and 431 verses.

Who reads it as Scripture. 1 Esdras stands at the head of the two Greek books of Ezra in the Septuagint, the Greek Old Testament, where Ezra–Nehemiah is the second. Orthodox churches that read the Greek Old Testament keep it in their Bibles, and the Ethiopian Orthodox Church counts it among its books. The Catholic Church does not count it as Scripture: the Council of Trent left it out, and the official Latin Bible of 1592 printed it as "3 Esdras" outside the canonical books. Anglicans read it among the Apocrypha, for example of life but not for doctrine, and the King James Version printed it. Other Protestants and Judaism do not count it as Scripture. Whether it belongs in the Old Testament is asked on the book card for Ezra; the canon section below gives each church's position in full.

Why read it. It is the oldest surviving witness to another form of the Ezra story, and it was the form the Jewish historian Josephus followed at the end of the first century AD. Read beside the Hebrew books, it shows how Jews of the centuries before Jesus told the story of the return: centered on the temple and its worship, on Josiah, Zerubbabel and Ezra, and on the law read aloud to all the people. Its story of the three guards gave the West a proverb, in its Latin form Magna est veritas et praevalet, "Great is truth, and it prevails."
facts: Orthodox churches that read the Greek Old Testament, where it is the first of the two books of Esdras (Greek and Russian Orthodox teachers rank it with the books that are not in the Hebrew Bible); the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church. Among the Apocrypha for Anglicans (read, not used for doctrine). Not Scripture for the Catholic Church (left out at Trent, 1546; printed in an appendix of the Latin Bible of 1592), for Lutheran, Reformed, Baptist and most other Protestant churches, or for Judaism.

1 Esdras in English Bibles (the KJV and most modern ones); Esdras A (Greek Esdras alpha) in the Septuagint; 3 Esdras in the Latin Vulgate and in the Church of England's Article VI, which call Ezra and Nehemiah 1 and 2 Esdras; 2 Esdras in Russian Bibles. On this site "2 Esdras" never means the Latin apocalypse, which is called 4 Ezra.
Unknown: the Jewish compiler or translator who put the Greek together from a Hebrew and Aramaic form of the Ezra story, with the story of the three guards, which may have had its own author.

Uncertain. Most scholars place the Greek in the 100s or first century BC, before Josephus used it (about AD 94). Torrey (1910) dated the Greek to the first century BC and the story of the guards, in its first form, to soon after 300 BC.
Jerusalem, Babylon and the Persian court, from Josiah's eighteenth year (622 BC, 1:20) to Ezra's reading of the law in the seventh year of a king Artaxerxes (usually dated 458 BC).
History retold: a Greek version of 2 Chronicles 35–36, Ezra 1–10 and Nehemiah 7:73–8:12, in its own order, with an added court tale and wisdom contest (3:1–5:6).
Greek, translated (except perhaps parts of the guards' story) from Hebrew and Aramaic. No Hebrew or Aramaic copy of the book itself survives.

Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), printed by Swete and followed by this site; Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), in Swete's notes; the Göttingen critical edition of Robert Hanhart (1974). In Vaticanus the book ends with the title "Esdras A," in Alexandrinus "Ezras A."
9 chapters, 431 verses (Swete's numbering, used on this site; the KJV divides the same text into 448 verses)
authorship: Early Christian writers quoted it under the name of Ezra (Esdras), as part of the Greek books of Ezra. Cyprian of Carthage (AD 256) quotes its praise of truth with "as it is written" and "in Esdras" (Letter 73.9), and Augustine read the contest as a prophecy of Christ, "the Truth" (City of God 18.36). Neither claims that Ezra wrote the Greek; the book itself names no author, and Ezra appears only in its last three chapters.

The book is a Greek translation, made from a Hebrew and Aramaic text close to, but not the same as, the one behind our Ezra–Nehemiah and the end of Chronicles, by a translator who wrote freer and more polished Greek than the translator of the Greek Ezra–Nehemiah (Esdras B). The story of the three guards (3:1–5:6) has no Hebrew parallel; most think it came from a separate source and was fitted into the history, with Zerubbabel's name added at 4:13 (Torrey). Who did the work, and where, is unknown.

Scholars divide over what the book is. Some see a surviving piece of an older Greek translation, or an older edition, of the whole Chronicles–Ezra–Nehemiah history: Charles C. Torrey (1910) called it "a rescued fragment of the old Greek translation of Chronicles-Ezra-Nehemiah." Others see a deliberate new work: Zipora Talshir (1999) argues that the story of the guards is the reason the book exists, and the reason for its different scope and order. H. St J. Thackeray's three options, as Swete sets them out, still frame the debate: a compilation from the Greek of Chronicles and Ezra–Nehemiah, a witness to an earlier Greek version, or an independent translation of an earlier Hebrew text. See "Beside Chronicles, Ezra and Nehemiah" below.

audience.to: Greek-speaking Jews of the last centuries before Jesus, who read their Scriptures in Greek: most likely in Egypt, where the Septuagint was made, or in the Jewish homeland itself; the book gives no clue to its place. They lived under Greek kings or Roman power, as heirs of the exiles who had come back to Judea under the Persians, and many of them lived abroad, as Daniel's and Zerubbabel's people had in Babylon. Their temple stood, rebuilt in the days the book describes. The first reader we can name is Josephus, a Jewish priest writing in Rome about AD 94, who followed this book rather than the Greek Ezra–Nehemiah for the story of the return, including the contest of the guards (Antiquities 11.31–67).
audience.why: To tell the story of the temple from its last great Passover before the exile to its rebuilding and the restoring of its worship and law, as one line of history. The book begins with Josiah keeping the Passover "by the LORD's command given to Moses" (1:6) and ends with all the people hearing the law, so its frame is worship and Torah, while Nehemiah and the city wall, which fill much of the Hebrew Nehemiah, are left out. The added contest shows a Jewish youth at a foreign court who wins by wisdom, as Daniel and Joseph do, and who uses the king's favor for Jerusalem; it tells readers living under foreign kings that truth, and "the God of truth" (4:40), are stronger than wine, kings and the power of women. Knowing the readers changes how the book reads: it is not a rival to Ezra for its first audience, but the Ezra story told in their language, with a hero their own age could admire.
views: Part of a larger Greek history

If the book is a surviving piece of a longer Greek translation of Chronicles–Ezra–Nehemiah (Torrey), its first readers had the whole history, and our book's limits, and its broken last sentence, are an accident of how it was copied.
A book made for its own purpose

If it was made as a book (Talshir), its compiler chose to begin with Josiah's Passover and end with the law read aloud, and built it around the story of the guards to honor Zerubbabel, the heir of David, as the one who won the rebuilding.

Some place the translator among the Jews of Egypt, others in Judea; the handbook of Bullard and Hatton notes that the place is not known, and most scholars settle only on a date, about the first century BC or a little earlier.

The first guard on wine; the second on the king
The third guard, Zerubbabel, on women, and on truth: "Great is truth"
Darius rewards Zerubbabel: letters for the rebuilding, the vessels, land and pay; the exiles rejoice in Babylon
The leaders who went up with Zerubbabel under Darius
The list of those who returned (Ezra 2)
The altar rebuilt, the Feast of Booths, the temple's foundation laid with shouts and weeping (Ezra 3)
The neighbors' offer refused; the work hindered (Ezra 4:1–5)

lenses.name: Orthodox
lenses.desc: Orthodox churches that read the Greek Old Testament keep 1 Esdras in their Bibles, beside Ezra and Nehemiah, as part of the story of the return from exile; Greek and Russian Orthodox teachers place it with the books not found in the Hebrew Bible, read for building up rather than for settling doctrine.

lenses.name: Historical-critical
lenses.desc: Most scholars read 1 Esdras as a Greek work made in the 100s or first century BC from a Hebrew and Aramaic form of the Ezra story, and ask whether it preserves an older edition of Ezra or reworks the one we have, and where the story of the three guards came from.

lenses.name: Jewish reception
lenses.desc: 1 Esdras is not in the Jewish Bible, and the rabbis do not use it, but the Jewish historian Josephus followed it in his Antiquities, including the story of the three guards, so some Jews of the first century AD read it as their history.

lenses.name: Beside Chronicles, Ezra and Nehemiah
lenses.desc: Reading 1 Esdras verse by verse beside the Hebrew books it retells: where it agrees, where it adds or leaves out, and where it changes names, numbers and order.

lenses.name: Western churches: read, not Scripture
lenses.desc: Catholic and Protestant readers, who do not count 1 Esdras as Scripture but have long printed and read it: as 3 Esdras in an appendix to the Latin Vulgate, and as 1 Esdras in the Apocrypha of English Bibles, where the Church of England reads it for example of life but not for doctrine.

sections.b:
Read it with Ezra open beside it. Nine-tenths of 1 Esdras retells 2 Chronicles 35–36, Ezra and Nehemiah 8, and this site's Plain keeps the wording of those books wherever the Greek says the same thing, so that the differences stand out. When a name is spelled differently (Sanassar and Samanassar for Sheshbazzar at 2:11 and 2:14, Sanabassar at 6:18; Attarates where Nehemiah 8:9 has the governor Nehemiah, 9:49), when a number changes, or when a line is added or missing, the notes and the S lens point it out.

Then watch the order. The book moves the letter to King Artaxerxes, which in Ezra 4:7–24 interrupts the story of the temple, to just after Cyrus's decree (2:15–25), so the work stops before it has started. Then, at a feast of Darius, the contest of the three guards wins a new decree, and only then does the list of returning exiles follow (5:7–45). The story reaches Ezra (8:1) and ends with Ezra's public reading of the law (9:37–55), with Nehemiah's own story left out.

Finally, read the contest of the guards (3:1–5:6) as what it is: a court tale and a wisdom speech, like the stories of Joseph before Pharaoh and of Daniel before Nebuchadnezzar. Its speeches on wine, the king and women are clever and earthy; its speech on truth ends, "Blessed be the God of truth!" (1 Esdras 4:40).

This is the S lens, and the central question about the book. H. B. Swete set out the parallels: 1 Esdras 1 is 2 Chronicles 35:1–36:21; 2:1–14 is Ezra 1; 2:15–25 is Ezra 4:7–24; 3:1–5:6 has no parallel; 5:7–70 is Ezra 2:1–4:5; chapters 6–7 are Ezra 5–6; 8:1–9:36 is Ezra 7:1–10:44; and 9:37–55 is Nehemiah 7:73–8:13. The two Greek books overlap: Esdras B, the Greek Ezra–Nehemiah, is a close, word-for-word translation of the Hebrew, while Esdras A, our book, is freer and better Greek.

How the two are related is one of the old problems of Septuagint study. Swete, following Thackeray, listed three answers: (1) 1 Esdras is a compilation made from the Greek of Chronicles and Ezra–Nehemiah; (2) it is based on an earlier Greek version of those books; (3) it is an independent translation of an earlier Hebrew text. Charles C. Torrey argued in 1910 that it is "a rescued fragment" of the old Greek translation of the whole Chronicler's history, a few quires plucked from the middle of a codex, beginning at 2 Chronicles 35:1 and ending with the first words of Nehemiah 8:13. Zipora Talshir argued in 1999 that the book was made around the story of the guards, which is its reason for being and explains its different scope and order, and that both the Hebrew of Ezra and the Hebrew behind 1 Esdras changed in similar ways as they were copied. Most scholars now agree, at least, that the translator worked from a Hebrew and Aramaic text, not from the Greek Ezra; whether that text was older or younger than ours is still argued.

So the book matters even to readers who do not count it as Scripture. Where it differs from the Hebrew (the order of the Persian kings, Ezra's title, the absence of Nehemiah at the reading of the law, 9:49), it may preserve an earlier form of the story, or it may show how one Jewish writer reshaped it. The notes give the case for each.

sections.h: The contest of the three guards
sections.b:
King Darius gives a great feast, then lies awake. His three young bodyguards agree that each will write down what is strongest, and that the king will reward the wisest answer. One writes "wine," one "the king," and the third, "Women are strongest, but truth wins over all things" (1 Esdras 3:12). In the morning each defends his answer before the king and his nobles. Wine confuses every mind and makes slave and king equal; the king rules all and is obeyed in everything; but women bear kings and the men who plant the vines, and men leave father and country for them, and the king's own concubine Apame slaps him and takes his crown while he smiles (4:29–31). Then the third youth praises truth: the earth is great and the sun swift, but truth endures, judges fairly, and "has the strength, the royal power, the authority and the majesty of all the ages" (1 Esdras 4:40). The people cry out, "Great is truth, and it is strongest!" (1 Esdras 4:41). The king makes the young man his "kinsman," and he asks for nothing for himself, only that Darius keep his vow to rebuild Jerusalem (4:42–46).

Only at 4:13 is the third guard named, in a short aside: he is Zerubbabel. Torrey judged that aside "secondary," a note that joins a once separate tale to the history, and argued that the tale was first composed in Aramaic, in Palestine, probably soon after 300 BC, as popular wisdom with no Jewish history in it; he found in it no quotation of the Old Testament, and thought the one possible echo, of Deuteronomy 10:17 at 4:39, accidental. Talshir, as above, thinks the book was built for this story. Either way, the story makes Zerubbabel, heir of David, the wise man whose words win the rebuilding, and it gives Darius, not Cyrus, the central decree. Swete called the scene "certainly unhistorical" in its present form, since Zerubbabel belonged to the age of Cyrus, and Cyrus decreed the rebuilding; the chapter pages weigh this.

The Latin of 4:41, magna veritas et praevalet ("great is truth, and it prevails"), became the proverb Magna est veritas et praevalet, which Swete called "immortal."

sections.h: The Persian kings in the wrong order?
sections.b:
Read as it stands, the book's order of kings is hard to follow. Cyrus sends the vessels (2:1–14); Artaxerxes stops the work (2:15–25); Darius rewards Zerubbabel and sends the exiles (3–5:6); the returning exiles then lay the foundation and are hindered "all the time of King Cyrus's life" for two years, until Darius (5:70); and in Darius's second year Haggai and Zechariah stir them to build again (6:1). In history the order was Cyrus (king of Babylon 539–530 BC), Cambyses, Darius I (522–486), Xerxes I (486–465), then Artaxerxes I (465–424), so a letter to Artaxerxes cannot have stopped a building that resumed under Darius I.

Ezra has a milder form of the same puzzle, since Ezra 4:6–23 tells of letters under Xerxes and Artaxerxes before returning to Darius at Ezra 4:24, "Then the work on God's house in Jerusalem stopped. It stayed stopped until the second year of the reign of Darius king of Persia" (Ezra 4:24). Most readers take Ezra 4:6–23 as a deliberate aside about later opposition to the city wall. 1 Esdras, by putting the letter before the guards' story, turns the aside into the main line of events. Josephus noticed the problem and solved it his own way: in his retelling the accusing letter goes to Cambyses, Cyrus's son (Antiquities 11.21–30). Torrey argued that Jewish writers of the Greek period, like the book of Daniel, placed a Darius before Cyrus and so misordered only one king; this is his theory, and the chapter pages give others.

The Jewish historian Josephus, writing about AD 94, retold the return from exile in Jewish Antiquities book 11, and he followed 1 Esdras, not the Greek Ezra–Nehemiah. He tells the contest of the guards at length (11.31–67), with touches of his own: Zerubbabel had an old friendship with Darius, Darius himself sets the questions, and truth is "immortal and eternal." He moves the accusing letter to Cambyses (11.21–30). He places Ezra under Xerxes (11.120) and tells the reading of the law at the Feast of Booths without naming Nehemiah (11.154–157), as 1 Esdras has no Nehemiah there (9:49), and he ends Ezra's story with his death and burial in Jerusalem (11.158). Swete suggests that Josephus preferred the book for its better Greek. His use shows that a learned Jewish priest of the first century read 1 Esdras as a trustworthy history of his people, though not, as far as he says, as a separate holy book.

English Bibles (KJV, NRSV): 1 EsdrasEzra, Nehemiah2 Esdras
Russian Bibles: 2 EzraEzra, Nehemiah3 Ezra

The Church of England's Article VI, which follows the Latin numbering, calls Ezra and Nehemiah "The First Book of Esdras" and "The Second Book of Esdras" among the canonical books, and lists "The Third Book of Esdras" first among the books read for example of life. The Russian Synodal Bible titles this book the second book of Ezra. The KJV, like the English Bibles since the Geneva Bible of 1560 (Bullard and Hatton), calls it 1 Esdras, as does this site. On this site "2 Esdras" never names the apocalypse; that book is 4 Ezra.

sections.h: In the early church and the Vulgate
sections.b:
Early Christian writers used the book freely. Swete lists Clement of Alexandria (Stromata 1.21), Origen (on John, book 6; Homilies on Joshua 9) and Cyprian. Cyprian, arguing in AD 256 that custom must give way to truth, wrote "knowing that in Esdras also the truth conquers, as it is written," and quoted its praise of truth (Letter 73.9; 4:38). Augustine thought Esdras might be read "as prophesying of Christ" in the contest, since the third youth showed that "the truth is victorious over all," and "Christ is the Truth" (City of God 18.36), recalling Jesus' words, "I am the way, the truth and the life" (John 14:6).

In the canon lists of the 300s, Origen (as Eusebius reports him) counts "Esdras, First and Second in one," and Athanasius writes "Ezra, the first and second are similarly one book." Swete read these lists as counting the two Greek books of Esdras together inside the twenty-two books of the Hebrew canon; the words themselves do not say which two books are meant, since Ezra and Nehemiah were also called first and second Esdras.

Jerome, translating from the Hebrew for his Latin Bible, set it aside. In his preface to Ezra he says that among the Hebrews Ezra and Nehemiah are one book, and that no one should "take delight in the dreams found in the apocryphal third and fourth books." Latin Bibles went on copying it, and when the Council of Trent fixed the Catholic list in 1546 it named only "the first book of Esdras, and the second which is entitled Nehemias." The official Latin Bible issued under Pope Clement VIII in 1592 printed 3 and 4 Esdras and the Prayer of Manasseh, which Trent "did not count among the canonical books," in an appendix "outside the series of canonical Scripture," as its preface says (Latin). Catholic translations made from the Vulgate followed it, and Catholic Bibles made from the original languages since then leave it out.

The last verse breaks off. Nehemiah 8 goes on after the feast of joy: "The next day the family heads of all the people, the priests and the Levites gathered to Ezra the scribe to gain insight into the words of the law" (Nehemiah 8:13). The Greek of 1 Esdras ends with the single word for "and they gathered" (9:55). Swete compared the ending of Mark at Mark 16:8; Torrey took it as proof that the book is a piece of a longer Greek history; Bullard and Hatton say all scholars assume more material once existed. Others think the compiler chose to close with the reading of the law, and that the last word was added later from Nehemiah 8:13. The ending is one of the strongest arguments that our book once belonged to something longer.

spec.title: Claude's theory: the contest answers Josiah's death
spec.body: The book opens with a good king who would not listen. The king of Egypt tells Josiah that the Lord is with him and that Josiah should not stand against the Lord, and Josiah goes out to fight anyway and dies (1:24–31). Where 2 Chronicles 35:22 says that Josiah "did not listen to Neco's words from God's mouth," 1 Esdras says that he did not listen to the words of Jeremiah the prophet from the mouth of the Lord (1:26). In the middle of the book a foreign king listens: Darius hears a young Jew speak about truth, and does what he is asked (4:42–57). My suggestion is that the compiler meant the two scenes to be read together. The story moves from a king of Judah who would not hear the word of God, though a prophet spoke it, to a king of Persia who hears the truth from a Jewish mouth; Josiah's deafness opens the slide to the exile, and Darius's hearing opens the rebuilding. I have not found this pairing in the scholarship I could check; it builds on Talshir's view that the guards' story is the center of the book.

spec.title: Claude's theory: why Nehemiah is missing
spec.body: 1 Esdras leaves out all of Nehemiah's own story, and at the reading of the law the one who speaks with Ezra is named Attarates, not Nehemiah (9:49; compare Nehemiah 8:9, where Nehemiah is "the governor"). Scholars have long asked whether Nehemiah's name was added to Nehemiah 8 later, or dropped here. My suggestion concerns the book as it now reads, whatever its history: with Nehemiah gone, the book has three founders, Josiah the king who kept the Passover, Zerubbabel the heir of David who won the temple, and Ezra the priest who gave back the law, and the city wall, Nehemiah's great work, plays no part. A book for Jews living under foreign kings, with no walls of their own, may have found its hope in worship and Torah rather than fortifications. This is a reading of the book's shape, not a claim about which text is older.

canon.summary: 1 Esdras is the first of the two books of Esdras in the Greek Old Testament, and Orthodox churches that read the Greek Bible keep it there, ranking it with the books not in the Hebrew Bible; the Ethiopian Orthodox Church counts it too. The Catholic Church left it out at Trent and prints it, if at all, only in an appendix; Anglicans read it among the Apocrypha, for example of life but not for doctrine; other Protestants and Judaism do not count it as Scripture.
accepted_by: In the Old Testament. Orthodox Bibles follow the Septuagint, where this book is Esdras A, the first of two Greek books of Esdras. The Romanian Orthodox scholar Alexandru Mihăilă counts it among the ten books beyond the Hebrew canon that the Orthodox reckon, and among the two of them that Catholics do not accept (with 3 Maccabees). Its rank has been explained in two ways, as for the other such books: as Scripture read with the rest of the Old Testament, and, following Athanasius, as among the books "appointed of the Fathers to be read" by those preparing for baptism, below the twenty-two books of the Hebrew canon. No council of all the Orthodox churches has fixed its place, and the Orthodox Church in America's answer on the canon, which names the other such books, does not name it.

In the Slavonic and Russian Bibles, where it is titled the second book of Ezra (the Synodal Bible's 2 Ezra), and 4 Ezra is printed as 3 Ezra. The Longer Catechism of Philaret of Moscow (1839) counts the twenty-two books of the Hebrew canon, with "the first book of Esdras, and the second, or, as it is entitled in Greek, the book of Nehemiah," and says the books not in the Hebrew were "appointed of the Fathers to be read by proselytes"; this book belongs to that second group.

Counted among its books. R. W. Cowley found 1 Esdras in the narrower form of the church's canon given in its prayer book, and in the deuterocanonical volume of the Ge'ez and Amharic Bible, beside Ezra and Nehemiah and the Ezra Apocalypse (4 Ezra).

Not Scripture. Jerome set the "third and fourth" books of Esdras aside as apocryphal. The Council of Trent's list (1546) has only "the first book of Esdras, and the second which is entitled Nehemias," and the Catechism lists "Ezra and Nehemiah" (120). The Clementine Vulgate of 1592 printed it, as 3 Esdras, outside the series of canonical books, because Trent had not counted it among them.

Among the Apocrypha. Article VI of the Thirty-Nine Articles lists "The Third Book of Esdras" first among the books that "the Church doth read for example of life and instruction of manners; but yet doth it not apply them to establish any doctrine," and the King James Version of 1611 printed it with the Apocrypha.

Not Scripture, and not even among Luther's Apocrypha. In his preface to Baruch (1534) Luther wrote that he had not wished to translate the third and fourth books of Esdras into German, "because they contain nothing that one could not find better in Aesop."

Not Scripture. The Belgic Confession (1561) lists "the third and fourth books of Esdras" first among the apocryphal books, which the church may read "as far as they agree with the canonical books"; the Westminster Confession says the Apocrypha, "not being of divine inspiration, are no part of the canon of Scripture" (1.3). Baptist and most other Protestant Bibles leave it out.
Not Scripture. No Hebrew or Aramaic copy of the book is known, and the rabbis do not cite it. Josephus used it as a source of history (Antiquities 11).

provenance.h: A Greek book from a Hebrew and Aramaic text
provenance.b: 1 Esdras survives in Greek, in the great codices of the Greek Bible: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), whose text this site follows in Swete's edition, and Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD). In Vaticanus the book closes with the title "Esdras A," in Alexandrinus "Ezras A," the first of two Greek books of Ezra. Its Greek was translated from a Hebrew and Aramaic text of Chronicles, Ezra and Nehemiah 8, close to the Hebrew we have but not the same: the Aramaic letters of Ezra 4–6 stand behind 2:15–25 and 6:1–7:15 here too. No Semitic copy of the book itself survives.

No one knows exactly. It must be older than Josephus, who used it about AD 94, and it reads like the work of the late Septuagint period. Bullard and Hatton report that most scholars are comfortable with the first century BC; others place it in the 100s BC. Torrey dated the Greek translation to the first century BC, and the story of the guards, in its first form, to Palestine soon after 300 BC. Whether the translator worked in Egypt or in Judea is unknown.

Most of the book is a free translation of passages we know from the Hebrew; its own material is the contest of the guards and the passage that joins it to the history (3:1–5:6), and a few lines on Josiah (1:21–22). Scholars still debate whether it is a fragment of a fuller Greek history (Torrey) or a book composed around the guards' story (Talshir). See the book page's section "Beside Chronicles, Ezra and Nehemiah."

rejected_why.b: Judaism's Bible has Chronicles, Ezra and Nehemiah, and nothing that corresponds to this book as a whole. Its one new story, the contest of the guards, survives only in Greek and in translations from the Greek. For Jews, and for the many Christians who hold that the Old Testament canon is the Hebrew Bible, that settles it. Jerome, who translated from the Hebrew, said so in his preface to Ezra: Ezra and Nehemiah are one book among the Hebrews, and the "third and fourth" books are apocryphal "dreams."

Since nine-tenths of the book retells Chronicles, Ezra and Nehemiah, a church that already reads those books gains little but the story of the guards and a different order of events. Where it differs, it raises problems: it sets the letter to Artaxerxes before Darius (2:15–25), and it has Darius send Zerubbabel back (4:47–5:6) where Ezra has Cyrus. Reformed and Lutheran writers who set it aside could point to these as signs that it is not a reliable copy of Scripture but a later retelling.

rejected_why.h: Left out where Western churches fixed their lists
rejected_why.b: The Council of Trent (1546) named the books it received "as they are contained in the old Latin vulgate edition," and its list had only two books of Esdras, Ezra and Nehemiah. The editors of the Clementine Vulgate (1592) then placed 3 and 4 Esdras and the Prayer of Manasseh outside the series of canonical books for that reason. Article VI (1571) and the Belgic Confession (1561) had already named it among the books read for example of life, but not for doctrine. Luther did not even translate it. The Westminster Confession (1646) denies the whole Apocrypha divine inspiration.

cited_in.b: No book of the 66 quotes 1 Esdras. Its first chapter retells 2 Chronicles 35–36 almost line by line, with a few lines about Josiah added (1:21–22). Scholars agree that 1 Esdras draws on this material, either from a Hebrew text of Chronicles or from an older edition of the Chronicler's history (Torrey); Chronicles does not depend on 1 Esdras.

Cyrus's decree and the return of the vessels with Sheshbazzar, here spelled Sanassar and Samanassar (2:11, 14). The decree's opening also ends 2 Chronicles 36:22–23, the place where the Hebrew books are stitched together; 1 Esdras runs on from Chronicles to Ezra with no break, one reason scholars think it reflects a single continuous history.

The officials' letter to Artaxerxes and his reply, moved here before the story of the guards. Whether the move was made by the compiler, or the Hebrew Ezra was rearranged, is debated (see the book page).
The list of those who returned, with many names and numbers spelled or counted differently in the Greek; the notes give the Hebrew forms. Nehemiah 7:6–73 repeats the same list.
The altar, the Feast of Booths, the foundation of the temple with shouts and weeping, and the neighbors whose help is refused.

Haggai and Zechariah, the inquiry of the governor (here Sisinnes), Darius's search for Cyrus's decree, the temple's completion and the Passover. The date of completion is the twenty-third of Adar here (7:5) but the third in Ezra 6:15.

Ezra's return with Artaxerxes' letter, his prayer over the mixed marriages, and the assembly that sends the foreign wives away; in 1 Esdras Ezra is called "high priest" at the reading of the law (9:39–40, 49), not in Ezra.

Ezra reads the law to all the people. The speaker at Ezra's side is Attarates here (9:49), where Nehemiah 8:9 names Nehemiah, and the book breaks off with the first word of Nehemiah 8:13, "and they gathered" (9:55).

Both books date the renewed building to the second year of Darius and name Zerubbabel and Jeshua (Joshua) as its leaders; Haggai and Zechariah are the 66 books' own witnesses to the Darius period that 1 Esdras 3–7 describes, and they never mention the contest of the guards.

reliability.verdict: As a witness to how Jews of the last centuries BC told the story of the return, 1 Esdras is valuable and early: Josephus trusted it, and it may preserve an older form of parts of Ezra. As a text, it is well kept in the great Greek codices but survives in no Semitic copy, and it ends mid-sentence. As history, where it matches Chronicles and Ezra it is as good as they are; where it departs, its order of Persian kings and its Darius-centered story of Zerubbabel are very hard to square with Haggai, Zechariah and the Persian record, and most historians judge the contest of the guards a court tale. Against the 66 books it is mostly a retelling, with one large addition and some real conflicts of order, names and dates, none of which touches doctrine.

sections.b: High. The book shows what a Greek-speaking Jewish compiler of about the first century BC thought mattered in the story of the return: the Passover kept rightly, the temple and its vessels, the house of David in Zerubbabel, the purity of the people, and the law read to all. Its praise of truth, ending in "Blessed be the God of truth!" (1 Esdras 4:40), shows Jewish wisdom speaking in the language of its Greek neighbors. Josephus's use of it, in the first century AD, shows that some Jews trusted it as history.

The Greek is well attested in Codex Vaticanus (300s AD) and Codex Alexandrinus (400s AD), which differ in many small readings (Swete's notes), and it was translated into Latin, Syriac, Ethiopic and other languages. There is no Hebrew or Aramaic copy, no Dead Sea Scroll of it, and no early papyrus. The last verse breaks off. The name at 4:13 may be a later note. Where the Greek and the Hebrew books differ, it is often unclear whether the translator read a different Hebrew text, misread his text, or changed it on purpose; scholars disagree verse by verse.

Where it follows Chronicles and Ezra it carries their history; the S lens and the notes show the small changes. Its own framework is a different matter. It has Artaxerxes stop the work before Darius (2:15–25), though Artaxerxes I reigned after Darius I; it has Darius send Zerubbabel with the exiles (4:47–5:6), where Ezra 1–3 and the decree found again in Ezra 6 (6:23–26 here) give the first return and decree to Cyrus; and it says the work was blocked for two years until Darius (5:70). Haggai and Zechariah, who preached in Darius's second year, speak to Zerubbabel as governor already in Judah (Haggai 1:1) and never mention a contest. Swete judged the story "certainly unhistorical" in its present form. Orthodox readers who keep the book in their Bibles have generally read it, with the rest of the Septuagint, for its witness to God's faithfulness in the return rather than as a chronicle to be set against Ezra, and some defenders of its history have suggested that Zerubbabel went to and from the Persian court more than once. Neither view can be proved from the sources we have.

sections.h: 4. Against the 66 books, point by point
sections.b: Agrees: almost all of chapters 1–2 and 5–9 say what 2 Chronicles 35–36, Ezra and Nehemiah 8 say, often word for word. Goes beyond: the contest of the guards and Zerubbabel's prayer (3:1–5:6); the lines on Josiah's piety (1:21–22); a thousand horsemen sent with the exiles (5:2). Conflicts: the order of the Persian kings; who sends Zerubbabel (Darius here, Cyrus in Ezra); the date the temple was finished (the twenty-third of Adar, 7:5, against the third, Ezra 6:15); Ezra called high priest (9:39–40, 49); the speaker at the reading named Attarates, not Nehemiah (9:49, Nehemiah 8:9). Doctrine: it teaches nothing about God, sin or salvation that the 66 books do not; its praise of truth echoes the Psalms and the prophets. So for churches that read it, it adds a story and a witness to the text, not a teaching; for churches that do not, its conflicts with Ezra are part of the reason.

how_to_read.h: As the Ezra story in another form
how_to_read.b: Read 1 Esdras with Ezra, and with the end of 2 Chronicles and Nehemiah 8, open beside it. Where it agrees, it is a second witness to their text; where it differs, ask whether it preserves an older form or reshapes the story, and see the notes. Do not use it to correct Ezra's history without weighing Haggai and Zechariah.

how_to_read.h: As a court tale and a wisdom speech
how_to_read.b: Read the contest of the guards (3:1–5:6) as the stories of Joseph, Daniel and Esther are read: a Jew at a foreign court who wins favor by wisdom and uses it for God's people. Enjoy its wit, then listen to its last speech, which turns from the strength of women to the God of truth.

Orthodox readers hear it in their Old Testament among the books read for building up. Ethiopian Orthodox readers count it among their books. Catholic and most Protestant readers can read it as Jerome, Article VI and the Belgic Confession allow, "for example of life" and "as far as they agree with the canonical books," and test it by them. Whether it belongs in the Old Testament at all is the question on the book card for Ezra (see the topic page on 1 Esdras).
